newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania slowly restores order with month-old govt.
newsitem.headline: Albania slowly restores order with month-old govt.

text.p: Gunfire still lights up the night sky and grisly killings are a regular feature of evening news broadcasts. But a month after Albania's slide into anarchy, the worst seems over.
The emergency government that came together on March 14 was a last-ditch effort to prevent a total breakdown of the Balkan state.

Its desperate calls for NATO peacekeepers to round up weapons that had fallen into civilian hands were ignored. But Prime Minister Bashkim Fino's 10-party government has nevertheless managed to steer back from the brink.
"The situation has improved, local authorities have the situation under control," Fino said. "Many (rebel) committees have been dissolved and the authorities have taken charge."

A multinational force of 6,000 troops is due to arrive on Tuesday. The U.N.-backed mission may be coming late and offering little -- their aim has been strictly limited to protecting humanitarian aid convoys.
But their arrival is still a huge, hopeful signal.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi was welcomed as a hero in Albania on Sunday. Italy will lead the eight-nation force and Prodi's visit raised hopes that Europe's poorest country will not, after all, be forgotten.

Prodi's bold visit was unthinkable last month because of local outrage over the sinking of a refugee boat off the coast of Italy. An Italian naval vessel had collided with the boat and at least 80 Albanians were killed in the disaster.

"This is a country of immense potential," Prodi said. "It has had a crisis. I hoped for a while that it could get over it alone. It has asked for our help. We'll give it, but I believe this country is capable of making great strides forward."

Nearly 300 people have been killed in the country of 3.4 million and more than 700 injured in Albania in a spasm of lawless terror that erupted in February after the collapse of get-rich-quick savings schemes wiped out the savings of thousands of families.

Many Albanians were killed in the south, where the popular uprising against President Sali Berisha began. Berisha, a former cardiologist to the hard-line communist rulers, was especially detested in the south.
The situation was bleak when Fino's crisis government was formed a month ago.
Army arsenals had been looted after soldiers and police deserted. The entire prison population of 1,309 escaped and many fleeing convicts set fire to their jails.
The offices of a leading independent newspaper in Tirana were ransacked. Enraged gangs stormed court buildings, prosecutors offices, city halls, and police stations.
American marines and German troops flying in by helicopter to evacuate their embassies fought pitched battles with gunmen on the ground.

At the height of the crisis, Berisha appointed an all-party emergency government headed by Fino, a former southern mayor from the opposition Socialist party. The new government has largely put political squabbling aside and is determined to hold new elections in June.

"A main objective of the government is setting up general elections in June that will be truly free and fair," government spokesman Jorgji Kote said. "The government of National Reconciliation was the only solution amid the chaos."

There are small but important signs that normality is gradually returning to Albania. Last week the government asked parliament to lift restrictions on the press that were imposed in early March and six newspapers quickly resumed publication.
Schools, which shut in early March, began opening on Monday in Tirana and the national soccer league is planning to restart the truncated season in cities that are now safely in government control.
The return of exiled King Leka to a thunderous welcome on Saturday was another signal for many Albanians that better days lie ahead.

Even though his father, King Zog, was ousted by invading Italian fascists 58 years ago -- when Leka was a mere two days old -- many Albanians have pinned their hopes on King Leka, who at 2.05 metres (6.5 feet) towers over most of his countrymen.
"In a country with no hope, he is hope," said one man hurrying to witness King Leka's arrival at Tirana airport.

But Albania's woes are far from over. Unemployment is too high to even be seriously counted, about three-quarters of the army's weapons are missing, much of the south is controlled by rebel town committees, and there is almost no public confidence in the justice system.
Bursts of automatic gunfire can be heard everywhere and the glow of tracer bullets light up Tirana's starry sky at night, frightening reminders that Albania is still far from safe.
